To further examine whether Gnal+/- mice exhibit constitutive motor deficit (taking into account gender), we performed a larger set of motor experiments, including vertical pole, horizontal bar, grid test, fixed-speed rotarod, gait test, and an open-field test (Figure 1, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is demonstrated by the behavioral tests shown in Figure 1 showing no significant differences between genotypes.

claims.claim: The motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test.
claims.source: We observed that the motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1a), horizontal bar test (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1a), and grid test (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A with no significant differences between genotypes.

claims.claim: The motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the horizontal bar test.
claims.source: We observed that the motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1a), horizontal bar test (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1a), and grid test (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1B with no significant differences between genotypes.

claims.claim: The motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the grid test.
claims.source: We observed that the motor performance of Gnal+/- mice was not impaired in the vertical pole test (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1a), horizontal bar test (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1a), and grid test (Figure 1C, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C with no significant differences between genotypes.

claims.claim: Females exhibited better performances in the horizontal bar test, regardless of their genotype.
claims.source: Females exhibited better performances in the horizontal bar test, regardless of their genotype.
claims.evidence: This is observed in Figure 1B showing a gender effect independent of genotype.

claims.claim: No significant differences were found between Gnal+/- and WT mice in the fixed-speed rotarod test.
claims.source: Motor coordination was also examined in a fixed-speed rotarod test. We did not find significant differences between Gnal+/- and WT mice (Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1a), nor when comparing males and females for each speed step (Figure 1E, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D-E with no significant differences.

claims.claim: No significant differences were found in gait width, alternation coefficient, linear movement, sigma, or length of stride in the gait test between Gnal+/- and WT mice.
claims.source: In the gait test, we found no significant differences in gait width, alternation coefficient, linear movement, sigma, or length of stride (Figure 1F, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F with no significant differences across multiple gait parameters.

claims.claim: No significant differences were observed between genotype and gender in median instantaneous speed or distance traveled in the open field.
claims.source: Finally, in spontaneous locomotion in the open field, we observed no significant differences between genotype and gender neither in median instantaneous speed nor in distance traveled (Figure 1G, J and K, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1J-K with no significant differences.

claims.claim: No significant differences were observed between genotypes or genders in thigmotaxis and time spent exploring the center of the open field.
claims.source: Additionally, we included an analysis of the thigmotaxis and time spent exploring the center of the open field and observed no significant differences between genotypes or genders in our mice (Figure 1H, I, Supplementary file 1a).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 1H-I with no significant differences.

claims.claim: Motor activity and motor coordination are not impaired in young 3–7-month-old Gnal+/- mice.
claims.source: In conclusion, motor activity and motor coordination are not impaired in young 3–7-month-old Gnal+/- mice; furthermore, no significant differences were observed between male and female Gnal+/- mice compared to their WT littermates, allowing us to merge genders in the following physiological experiments.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on all the behavioral tests shown in Figure 1.

claims.claim: No significant differences were observed between male and female Gnal+/- mice compared to their WT littermates in motor tests.
claims.source: In conclusion, motor activity and motor coordination are not impaired in young 3–7-month-old Gnal+/- mice; furthermore, no significant differences were observed between male and female Gnal+/- mice compared to their WT littermates, allowing us to merge genders in the following physiological experiments.
claims.evidence: This is based on the analysis of gender effects across all behavioral tests in Figure 1.

claims.claim: VAL, CL, and M1 neurons presented no differences in firing rate between WT and Gnal+/- mice in basal conditions.
claims.source: VAL, CL, and M1 neurons presented no differences in firing rate between WT and Gnal+/- mice in basal conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A comparing baseline firing rates.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine treatment induces in both WT and Gnal+/- mice a cholinergic shock, which translates into excessive salivation and lacrimation, as well as a persistent immobility.
claims.source: As described previously, this treatment induces in both genotypes a cholinergic shock, which translates into excessive salivation and lacrimation, as well as a persistent immobility.
claims.evidence: This is an observation from the behavioral effects of oxotremorine administration.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine induces in Gnal+/- mice abnormal dystonic-like movements and postures.
claims.source: It also induces in Gnal+/- mice abnormal dystonic-like movements and postures.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the behavioral assessment and shown in Figure 5G.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine-treated mice presented a significant decrease in the firing rate of VAL and M1 neurons.
claims.source: Oxotremorine-treated mice, whether WT or Gnal+/-, presented a significant decrease in the firing rate of VAL and M1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A comparing firing rates before and after oxotremorine.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine did not modify the firing properties of CL neurons in WT mice.
claims.source: While oxotremorine did not modify the firing properties of CL neurons in WT mice, it decreased the firing rate of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A with a genotype-specific effect in CL.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine decreased the firing rate of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice.
claims.source: While oxotremorine did not modify the firing properties of CL neurons in WT mice, it decreased the firing rate of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, Supplementary file 1k and l).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine decreased the CVisi of VAL neurons in both WT and Gnal+/- mice.
claims.source: We observed a significant decrease in CVisi of VAL neurons in both WT and Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1o and p).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A measuring firing regularity.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine did not modify the CVisi of CL neurons in WT mice.
claims.source: While oxotremorine did not modify the CVisi of CL neurons in WT mice, it was decreased for CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1o and p), suggesting an increased regularity of firing.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine decreased the CVisi of CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice, suggesting an increased regularity of firing.
claims.source: While oxotremorine did not modify the CVisi of CL neurons in WT mice, it was decreased for CL neurons in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, Supplementary file 1o and p), suggesting an increased regularity of firing.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A with interpretation of the CVisi decrease.

claims.claim: The DN is the main output of the cerebellum towards the thalamus.
claims.source: The DN is the main output of the cerebellum towards the thalamus and is known to project both to the VAL and CL (Ichinohe et al., 2000; Teune et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge cited from the literature.

claims.claim: The DN projects to both the VAL and CL.
claims.source: The DN is the main output of the cerebellum towards the thalamus and is known to project both to the VAL and CL (Ichinohe et al., 2000; Teune et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge cited from the literature.

claims.claim: In naive saline-treated mice, VAL, CL thalamus and M1 neurons displayed significant departure from baseline firing during 100 ms DN stimulations in both WT and Gnal+/- mice.
claims.source: In naive saline-treated mice, we found a significant increase in firing rate for the VAL, CL thalamus and M1 neurons during 100 ms DN stimulations in WT and Gnal+/-mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B-C demonstrating responses to DN stimulation.

claims.claim: Responses in the VAL to DN stimulation were significantly larger in Gnal+/- than in WT mice in the presymptomatic state.
claims.source: Responses in the VAL were significantly larger in Gnal+/- than in WT mice, suggesting an increased responsiveness of this thalamo-cortical pathway in the presymptomatic state.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C comparing genotypes.

claims.claim: Low-frequency stimulation of the DN did not induce plastic changes of the responses in VAL, CL, and M1.
claims.source: We verified the absence of plastic changes of the responses in VAL, CL, and M1 induced by our low-frequency stimulation of the DN by showing the absence of significant difference between the average response to the first half of the stimulations ('early') and the second half of the stimulations ('late,' Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and D, Supplementary file 1n).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D comparing early and late responses.

claims.claim: The first exposure to oxotremorine does not cause significant short-term changes in the cerebellar drive of thalamic nuclei and motor cortex.
claims.source: We did not observe any significant difference in response to DN stimulation in the VAL, CL, and M1 in comparison to naive condition, for both genotypes (Supplementary file 1c and d). This suggests that the first exposure to oxotremorine does not cause significant short-term changes in the cerebellar drive of thalamic nuclei and motor cortex.
claims.evidence: This is based on the comparison of responses in the 'Oxo' condition to the naive condition.

claims.claim: Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state (Post-Oxo) presented a significantly larger response to DN stimulations in all recorded structures compared to the changes induced by oxotremorine in WT animals.
claims.source: While the acute exposure to oxotremorine yielded slightly increased responses in VAL neurons and decreased responses in M1 neurons in WT mice, Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state presented a significantly larger response to DN stimulations in all recorded structures compared to the changes induced by oxotremorine in WT animals (Figure 2C, Supplementary file 1c and d), indicating an increased excitability of the cerebello-thalamic pathways in asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice following the first dystonia induction.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 2C comparing Post-Oxo responses between genotypes.

claims.claim: A single exposure of Gnal+/- mice to oxotremorine induces long-lasting functional alterations in the cerebello-thalamic pathways that are more pronounced than the mild alterations observed in the presymptomatic state.
claims.source: Overall, these results show that a single exposure of Gnal+/- mice to oxotremorine induces, in the cerebello-thalamic pathways, long-lasting functional alterations that are more pronounced than the mild alterations observed in the presymptomatic state.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comparison of naive and Post-Oxo conditions in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: In saline-treated WT mice, θ-burst stimulations of the DN induced a potentiation of the response in VAL and M1 neurons to low-frequency stimulation.
claims.source: In saline-treated WT mice, the comparison of the increase in firing rate induced by DN stimulations before and after θ-burst stimulations (Figure 3B and C) revealed a potentiation of the response in VAL and M1 neurons to the low-frequency stimulation (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1e).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D demonstrating potentiation in WT mice.

claims.claim: In Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations failed to induce a significant potentiation in the responses of VAL, CL, or M1 neurons to DN stimulations in saline condition.
claims.source: On the other hand, in Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations failed to induce a significant potentiation in the responses of VAL, CL, or M1 neurons to DN stimulations, yielding significantly smaller θ-burst-induced changes in response to DN stimulations compared to WT mice (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1e).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3D comparing the effect of θ-burst between genotypes.

claims.claim: θ-burst stimulations of the DN induced a potentiated response for WT mice in motor thalamo-cortical pathways in saline condition, whereas this potentiation was absent in Gnal+/- mice.
claims.source: Hence, in the saline condition, θ-burst stimulations of the DN induced a potentiated response for WT mice in motor thalamo-cortical pathways, whereas this potentiation was absent in Gnal+/- mice, indicating an impaired plasticity of cerebello-thalamic pathways in the asymptomatic state.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings in Figure 3D-E.

claims.claim: The cerebello-CL-striatal pathway plays a central role in certain forms of dystonia.
claims.source: The cerebello-CL-striatal pathway (Ichinohe et al., 2000; Bostan and Strick, 2010; Chen et al., 2014; Gornati et al., 2018; Xiao et al., 2018) has been shown to play a central role in certain forms of dystonia (Chen et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: This is cited from studies on the cerebello-striatal pathway in dystonia.

claims.claim: DN neurons exhibited a bimodal distribution of firing rate in the DLS, allowing separation of slow- and fast-spiking neurons corresponding to putative medium spiny neurons and interneurons.
claims.source: DLS neurons exhibited a bimodal distribution of firing rate (Figure 4E), allowing to separate slow- and fast-spiking neurons corresponding to putative medium spiny neurons and interneurons (Her et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4E and based on established classification criteria cited from the literature.

claims.claim: Neurons from both slow- and fast-spiking populations in the DLS displayed significant departure from baseline firing during DN optogenetic stimulations in both WT and Gnal+/- mice.
claims.source: Neurons from both populations in the DLS displayed significant departure from baseline firing during DN optogenetic stimulations in both WT and Gnal+/- mice, but there was no significant increase in the firing rate of the population over the whole stimulation interval (Figure 4F, Supplementary file 1f).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4F demonstrating responses to DN-CL stimulation.

claims.claim: θ-burst stimulations of the DN produced a rhythmic entrainment of the DLS fast-spiking populations.
claims.source: Θ-burst stimulations of the DN also produced a rhythmic entrainment of the DLS fast-spiking populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C) consistent with a striatal entrainment through CL-projecting DN neurons.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-C.

claims.claim: In WT animals, DLS fast-spiking neurons exhibited increased responses to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations after θ-burst protocol.
claims.source: In WT animals, DLS fast-spiking neurons exhibited increased responses to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations after θ-burst protocol, not only when taking into account the whole duration of the DN stimulation (Figure 4H and I), but also when focusing on the initial response (Figure 4J).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I-J demonstrating potentiation in WT mice.

claims.claim: θ-burst DN stimulations increase the recruitment of DLS fast-spiking units through an oligo-synaptic pathway in WT mice.
claims.source: This suggests that θ-burst DN stimulations increase the recruitment of DLS fast-spiking units through an oligo-synaptic pathway.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the potentiation observed in Figure 4I-J.

claims.claim: The change in response to DN low-frequency 100 ms stimulations following θ-burst stimulations was absent in Gnal+/- mice in either type of units in the DLS.
claims.source: In contrast, such change in response to DN low-frequency 100 ms stimulations was absent in Gnal+/- mice in either type of units in the DLS following θ-burst stimulations.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 4I-J comparing the effect of θ-burst between genotypes.

claims.claim: The observed difference between genotypes in striatal plasticity is consistent with the impact of θ-burst stimulations in the CL neurons in saline condition.
claims.source: This observed difference between genotypes is consistent with the impact of θ-burst stimulations in the CL neurons in saline condition (Figure 3D and E) and thus indicates an impairment in cerebello-thalamo-striatal plasticity in asymptomatic ('post-Oxo') Gnal+/- mice.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation linking the striatal findings to the thalamic findings.

claims.claim: Following oxotremorine administration, the increase in firing rate in response to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1 neurons was stronger in Gnal+/- mice than WT mice.
claims.source: Following oxotremorine administration, the increase in firing rate in response to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1 neurons was stronger in Gnal+/- mice than WT mice (Figure 5B), as also found in the asymptomatic condition (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B comparing responses between genotypes in oxotremorine condition.

claims.claim: In WT mice, θ-burst stimulations under oxotremorine did not induce lasting changes in the response of VAL and M1 neurons to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations.
claims.source: In WT mice, θ-burst stimulations under oxotremorine did not induce lasting changes in the response of VAL and M1 neurons to low-frequency 100 ms DN stimulations, neither when taking into account the whole duration of stimulation (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 1i), nor when looking only at the initial response ('afferent volley,' Figure 5F, Supplementary file 1i).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E-F for WT mice in oxotremorine condition.

claims.claim: θ-burst stimulations in Gnal+/- mice under oxotremorine induced a lasting depression of the response to low-frequency cerebellar stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1.
claims.source: In contrast, θ-burst stimulations in Gnal+/- mice induced a lasting depression of the response to low-frequency cerebellar stimulations in VAL, CL, and M1 for the whole duration of the stimulation (Figure 5C–E, Supplementary file 1i).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C-E demonstrating depression in Gnal+/- mice.

claims.claim: The depression of responses to DN stimulation after θ-burst in Gnal+/- mice under oxotremorine was also observed in the afferent volley.
claims.source: This depression was also observed in the afferent volley (Figure 5F, Supplementary file 1i).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F analyzing the initial response window.

claims.claim: θ-bursts applied in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice induce a decrease in the entrainment of the thalamus and M1 by the cerebellum.
claims.source: Thus, while cerebellar drive of the thalamus and cortex is enhanced in asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice, θ-bursts applied in symptomatic (but not asymptomatic, Figure 3E and F) Gnal+/- mice induce a decrease in the entrainment of the thalamus and M1 by the cerebellum.
claims.evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the findings in Figure 5E-F compared to Figure 3.

claims.claim: In Gnal+/- mice, oxotremorine consistently induced abnormal postures such as the extension of hind limbs from the body axis for >10 s, sustained hunched posture with little movements, slow walking with increased hind limb gait, yielding maximal dystonia scores.
claims.source: In Gnal+/- mice, oxotremorine consistently induced abnormal postures such as the extension of hind limbs from the body axis for >10 s, sustained hunched posture with little movements, slow walking with increased hind limb gait, yielding maximal dystonia scores, while only mild motor signs were observed in WT mice (Figure 5H, Supplementary file 1j).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5G-H demonstrating the dystonic phenotype.

claims.claim: Only mild motor signs were observed in WT mice following oxotremorine administration.
claims.source: In Gnal+/- mice, oxotremorine consistently induced abnormal postures such as the extension of hind limbs from the body axis for >10 s, sustained hunched posture with little movements, slow walking with increased hind limb gait, yielding maximal dystonia scores, while only mild motor signs were observed in WT mice (Figure 5H, Supplementary file 1j).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H comparing dystonia scores between genotypes.

claims.claim: The surgical interventions (electrode and optical fiber implantation, AAV infections) did not impact the development of dystonic-type motor abnormalities in Gnal+/- mice.
claims.source: These observations are consistent with the previous findings in Gnal+/- mice (Pelosi et al., 2017) and indicate that the surgical interventions (electrode and optical fiber implantation, AAV infections) did not impact the development of dystonic-type motor abnormalities.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the consistency of the phenotype with prior reports.

claims.claim: DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decreased the abnormal motor state in Gnal+/- mice following oxotremorine injection.
claims.source: DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decreased the abnormal motor state in Gnal+/- mice following oxotremorine injection (Figure 5H).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5H comparing dystonia scores before and after θ-burst.

claims.claim: In saline-treated WT mice, DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations had no significant effect on the active wake time.
claims.source: In the saline-treated WT mice, DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations had no significant effect on the active wake time.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I for WT mice in saline condition.

claims.claim: In asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations did not significantly change the percentage of time spent in active wake.
claims.source: Similarly, in the asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice, θ-burst stimulations did not significantly change the percentage of time spent in active wake (Figure 5I, Supplementary file 1j).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I for Gnal+/- mice in saline condition.

claims.claim: In the oxotremorine condition, the average active wake time decreased in both WT and Gnal+/- mice compared to saline, the effect being more pronounced in the mutant mice.
claims.source: In contrast, in the oxotremorine condition, the average active wake time decreased in both WT and Gnal+/- mice compared to saline, the effect being more pronounced in the mutant mice (Figure 5I).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I comparing active wake between conditions.

claims.claim: One session of DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulation was sufficient to increase the time spent in active wake in Gnal+/- mice under oxotremorine.
claims.source: One session of DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulation was sufficient to increase the time spent in active wake in Gnal+/- mice (Figure 5I, Supplementary file 1j).
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5I comparing active wake before and after θ-burst in oxotremorine condition.

claims.claim: DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decrease the dystonic phenotype in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice regarding both the abnormal motor scores and active wake deficit.
claims.source: Overall, these results indicate that DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulations decrease the dystonic phenotype in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice regarding both the abnormal motor scores and active wake deficit.
claims.evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the findings in Figure 5H-I.

claims.claim: Young adult Gnal+/- mice in the presymptomatic state exhibit altered cerebello-thalamic functional connectivity without overt motor impairment.
claims.source: Our results show that young adult Gnal+/- mice in the presymptomatic state, that is, without overt motor impairment, already exhibit altered cerebello-thalamic functional connectivity.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from Figures 1 and 2.

claims.claim: After the first dystonic episode, mutant animals in the asymptomatic state exhibit further functional alterations of the cerebello-thalamic pathways with a marked increase in cerebello-thalamic excitability.
claims.source: After the first dystonic episode triggered by a cholinergic agonist, mutant animals, once returned to an asymptomatic state, exhibit further functional alterations of the cerebello-thalamic pathways, with a marked increase in cerebello-thalamic excitability and loss of potentiation of these functional connections by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations, which are also reflected downstream in the motor cortex and striatum.
claims.evidence: This is a summary of the findings in Figures 2 and 3.

claims.claim: After the first dystonic episode, mutant animals in the asymptomatic state exhibit loss of potentiation of cerebello-thalamic functional connections by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations.
claims.source: After the first dystonic episode triggered by a cholinergic agonist, mutant animals, once returned to an asymptomatic state, exhibit further functional alterations of the cerebello-thalamic pathways, with a marked increase in cerebello-thalamic excitability and loss of potentiation of these functional connections by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations, which are also reflected downstream in the motor cortex and striatum.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 3 demonstrating impaired plasticity.

claims.claim: Cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state induce a functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway absent from control mice.
claims.source: Finally, cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state induce a functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway absent from control mice, and this effect is accompanied by a reduction of the motor symptoms.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 demonstrating depression and symptom reduction.

claims.claim: The functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway induced by cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state is accompanied by a reduction of motor symptoms.
claims.source: Finally, cerebellar θ-burst stimulations in the symptomatic state induce a functional depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway absent from control mice, and this effect is accompanied by a reduction of the motor symptoms.
claims.evidence: This is shown in Figure 5 with both physiological and behavioral improvements.

claims.claim: In Gnal+/- mice before the first dystonia episode, the cerebello-thalamic tract exhibits an increased excitability that is amplified after the first episode and can be seen as a functional endophenotype.
claims.source: This shows that in Gnal+/- mice before the first dystonia episode the cerebello-thalamic tract exhibits an increased excitability that is amplified after the first episode and can thus be seen as a functional endophenotype.
claims.evidence: This is an interpretation of the progressive changes observed across conditions in Figure 2.

claims.claim: The plasticity induced in the cerebello-thalamic pathway via cerebellar stimulations reducing the cerebello-thalamic excitability exerts an effective therapeutic potential.
claims.source: Indeed, the plasticity induced in this pathway via cerebellar stimulations reducing the cerebello-thalamic excitability exerts an effective therapeutic potential.
claims.evidence: This is based on the therapeutic effects shown in Figure 5.

claims.claim: DYT25 is an adult-onset dystonia with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years).
claims.source: DYT25 is known to be an adult-onset dystonia, with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years), and, although the onset occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%), dystonia can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases (Fuchs et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013; Dufke et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2014; Ziegan et al., 2014; Saunders-Pullman et al., 2014; Carecchio et al., 2016; Dos Santos et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from multiple clinical reports on DYT25.

claims.claim: The onset of DYT25 occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%).
claims.source: DYT25 is known to be an adult-onset dystonia, with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years), and, although the onset occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%), dystonia can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases (Fuchs et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013; Dufke et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2014; Ziegan et al., 2014; Saunders-Pullman et al., 2014; Carecchio et al., 2016; Dos Santos et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from clinical reports on DYT25.

claims.claim: DYT25 can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases.
claims.source: DYT25 is known to be an adult-onset dystonia, with an age at onset ranging from 7 to 63 years (average of about 30 years), and, although the onset occurs mainly in the neck (about 80%), dystonia can affect various body parts, with generalization in 10% of the cases (Fuchs et al., 2013; Miao et al., 2013; Vemula et al., 2013; Dufke et al., 2014; Kumar et al., 2014; Ziegan et al., 2014; Saunders-Pullman et al., 2014; Carecchio et al., 2016; Dos Santos et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is cited from clinical reports on DYT25.

claims.claim: Immunohistochemistry study in rats reveals Gα(olf) labeling in the olfactory bulb, striatum, substantia nigra, and cerebellar cortex.
claims.source: Interestingly, the immunohistochemistry study in rats of Gα(olf), the protein encoded by Gnal, reveals labeling in the olfactory bulb, striatum, substantia nigra, and cerebellar cortex (Vemula et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from an expression study of Gα(olf).

claims.claim: In the striatum, Gα(olf) is closely associated with the G protein subunits, Gγ7 and Gβ2, and the type 5 adenylyl cyclase (AC5) to form a multi-molecular complex critical for cAMP production.
claims.source: In the striatum, Gα(olf) is closely associated with the G protein subunits, Gγ7 and Gβ2, and the type 5 adenylyl cyclase (AC5) to form a multi-molecular complex critical for cAMP production (Hervé, 2011; Xie et al., 2015) and mutations of Gγ7 and AC5 cause motor disorders, including dystonia, in animals and humans.
claims.evidence: This is cited from studies on the molecular complex involving Gα(olf).

claims.claim: Mutations of Gγ7 and AC5 cause motor disorders, including dystonia, in animals and humans.
claims.source: In the striatum, Gα(olf) is closely associated with the G protein subunits, Gγ7 and Gβ2, and the type 5 adenylyl cyclase (AC5) to form a multi-molecular complex critical for cAMP production (Hervé, 2011; Xie et al., 2015) and mutations of Gγ7 and AC5 cause motor disorders, including dystonia, in animals and humans.
claims.evidence: This is cited from studies on related genes in the same pathway.

claims.claim: Homozygous Gγ7 knockout mice display age-dependent dystonia.
claims.source: Homozygous Gγ7 knockout mice, which have a severe impairment of Gα(olf) signaling in the striatum, display age-dependent dystonia (Sasaki et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is cited from a study on Gγ7 knockout mice.

claims.claim: Loss-of-function mutations of ADCY5 are responsible for chorea with dystonia.
claims.source: In addition, loss-of-function mutations of ADCY5, the human gene encoding AC5, are responsible for chorea with dystonia (Carapito et al., 2015), whereas gain-of-function mutations cause dyskinesia with facial myokymia (Chen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from genetic studies in humans.

claims.claim: Gain-of-function mutations of ADCY5 cause dyskinesia with facial myokymia.
claims.source: In addition, loss-of-function mutations of ADCY5, the human gene encoding AC5, are responsible for chorea with dystonia (Carapito et al., 2015), whereas gain-of-function mutations cause dyskinesia with facial myokymia (Chen et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: This is cited from genetic studies in humans.

claims.claim: The anomalously high responsiveness of VAL neurons to cerebellar stimulations in Gnal+/- mice likely results at least in part from increased synaptic transmission or postsynaptic excitability.

claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the increased responses without increased DN activity.

claims.claim: Oxotremorine injections affected both control and Gnal+/- mice, but induced dystonic postures only in the mutant mice.

claims.claim: The oxotremorine-induced reduction of firing in the CL of Gnal+/- mice most likely reflects abnormal activity in the thalamo-striatal pathway in relation with dystonic symptoms.

Since only Gnal+/- mice expressed a strong dystonic phenotype, an oxotremorine-induced reduction of firing may correspond to a rather nonspecific effect of the cholinergic stimulation in the DN, VAL, and M1 while the specific change in the CL of Gnal+/- most likely reflects abnormal activity in the thalamo-striatal pathway in relation with dystonic symptoms.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on the genotype-specific effect in CL.

claims.evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from Figure 2.

claims.claim: Identifying cerebellar stimulation patterns that maximize the depression of the cerebello-thalamic pathway in patients could help improve therapeutic interventions.

results.result: Young adult (3-7 months old) Gnal+/- mice do not exhibit constitutive motor impairments. Comprehensive behavioral testing including vertical pole, horizontal bar, grid test, fixed-speed rotarod, gait analysis, and open-field tests showed no significant differences between Gnal+/- and WT mice, with the exception of a gender effect in the horizontal bar test independent of genotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C49 are well-supported by comprehensive behavioral data shown in Figure 1. Multiple motor tests consistently show no genotype-specific deficits, with appropriate statistical analyses (Kruskal-Wallis tests with post-hoc corrections). The sample sizes are adequate (n=11-27 per group), and the conclusion that young Gnal+/- mice represent a presymptomatic model is justified.

results.result: In the presymptomatic state, Gnal+/- mice exhibit increased cerebello-thalamic excitability. While baseline firing rates in VAL, CL, and M1 neurons were similar between genotypes, responses to DN optogenetic stimulation were significantly larger in VAL neurons of Gnal+/- mice compared to WT mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C50, C61, C62, and C4 are supported by electrophysiological data in Figure 2 and supplements. The finding of normal baseline firing but enhanced evoked responses in VAL specifically indicates altered functional connectivity rather than general hyperexcitability. Statistical comparisons are appropriate and the interpretation is conservative.

results.result: Oxotremorine administration induces genotype-specific and region-specific changes in neuronal activity. While both genotypes showed decreased firing in VAL and M1, only Gnal+/- mice showed decreased firing rate and CVisi in CL neurons, suggesting increased regularity of firing in this thalamo-striatal pathway specifically associated with dystonic symptoms.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C58 are supported by paired comparisons in Figure 2 supplements showing differential effects of oxotremorine between genotypes. The CL-specific effect in Gnal+/- mice is particularly notable and statistically significant. However, the interpretation that this reflects dystonia-related pathology (C131) requires caution as it's correlative.

results.result: Low-frequency DN stimulation does not induce plastic changes in cerebello-thalamic responses. Comparison of early versus late stimulation trials showed no significant differences, and acute oxotremorine exposure did not cause short-term changes in cerebellar drive of thalamic nuclei and motor cortex.
results.evaluation: Claims C63-C64 are supported by the control analyses in Figure 2 supplement 2D and statistical comparisons. This is an important methodological validation showing that the low-frequency stimulation protocol itself does not confound the plasticity measurements in subsequent experiments.

results.result: Following the first dystonic episode, Gnal+/- mice in the asymptomatic state (Post-Oxo) exhibit a marked and lasting increase in cerebello-thalamic excitability. Responses to DN stimulation in VAL, CL, and M1 were significantly larger in Post-Oxo Gnal+/- mice compared to both naive Gnal+/- mice and WT mice in any condition.
results.evaluation: Claims C65, C66, and C5 are strongly supported by Figure 2C showing progressive amplification of responses across conditions. The Post-Oxo state represents a persistent functional alteration (48-72 hours after oxotremorine), distinguishing it from acute drug effects. Statistical comparisons with interaction terms support genotype-specific progression.

results.result: Cerebello-thalamic plasticity is impaired in asymptomatic Gnal+/- mice. While θ-burst stimulation of DN induced lasting potentiation of responses in VAL and M1 neurons in WT mice, this potentiation was absent in Gnal+/- mice, indicating impaired plasticity of cerebello-thalamic pathways in the asymptomatic state.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69, C6, and C94 are supported by Figure 3D-E showing clear genotype differences in plasticity induction. The failure to potentiate in Gnal+/- mice is statistically significant and consistent across multiple downstream structures. The interpretation of impaired plasticity is appropriate, though the mechanism (saturation vs. other deficits) remains speculative (C149).

results.result: The cerebello-striatal pathway shows altered plasticity in Gnal+/- mice. DLS neurons exhibited bimodal firing rate distribution allowing classification into slow- and fast-spiking populations. In WT mice, θ-burst DN stimulation induced potentiation of fast-spiking neuron responses, but this potentiation was absent in Gnal+/- mice, indicating impaired cerebello-thalamo-striatal plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C77 are supported by Figure 4 showing classification of striatal neurons and differential plasticity responses. The bimodal distribution and classification criteria are appropriate (citing Her et al., 2016). The genotype difference in plasticity is consistent with thalamic findings (C77), though the exact mechanism remains unclear (C164 is speculative).

results.result: θ-burst stimulation in the symptomatic state induces genotype-specific depression of cerebello-thalamic responses. In Gnal+/- mice under oxotremorine, θ-burst stimulation induced lasting depression of responses in VAL, CL, and M1, while WT mice showed no lasting changes. This depression was observed in both the full response and the afferent volley.
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C82, C7, and C95 are strongly supported by Figure 5B-F showing state-dependent and genotype-specific plasticity. The depression in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice contrasts with the absence of potentiation in asymptomatic mice, suggesting that the cholinergic state enables a different form of plasticity. Statistical analyses are appropriate with paired comparisons.

results.result: θ-burst stimulation of DN reduces dystonic symptoms in Gnal+/- mice. Oxotremorine induced severe dystonic postures in Gnal+/- mice but only mild signs in WT mice. DN optogenetic θ-burst stimulation decreased both abnormal motor scores and active wake deficit in symptomatic Gnal+/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C83-C86, C8, C91, and C96 are supported by Figure 5G-I showing behavioral improvements. The dystonia scoring was blinded and used established scales. The therapeutic effect is modest but statistically significant and correlates with the physiological depression of cerebello-thalamic responses. Sample sizes are adequate (n=11-14).

results.result: The effect of θ-burst stimulation on active wake is state- and genotype-dependent. θ-burst had no effect in saline-treated mice of either genotype, but in the oxotremorine condition, active wake decreased in both genotypes (more in Gnal+/-), and one session of θ-burst stimulation increased active wake in Gnal+/- mice.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C90 are supported by Figure 5I showing differential effects across conditions. The active wake measure provides an objective complement to the dystonia scoring. The state-dependence of the therapeutic effect is consistent with the physiological findings, though the effect size is modest.

results.result: The study identifies increased cerebello-thalamic excitability as an early endophenotype in DYT25 dystonia. Young adult Gnal+/- mice show altered cerebello-thalamic functional connectivity without overt motor impairment, which is further amplified after the first dystonic episode, representing a progressive functional endophenotype.
results.evaluation: Claims C92, C93, C97, C9, and C176 represent the main conceptual conclusion integrating findings from multiple experiments. The progression from mild presymptomatic alterations to marked post-episode changes is well-documented. The term 'endophenotype' is appropriate for a subclinical marker, though its predictive value for symptom development requires longitudinal studies.

results.result: Depression of cerebello-thalamic pathways represents a therapeutic mechanism. The plasticity induced via cerebellar θ-burst stimulations that reduces cerebello-thalamic excitability exerts therapeutic potential, suggesting that identifying stimulation patterns that maximize this depression could improve therapeutic interventions.
results.evaluation: Claims C98, C10, C160, and C178 are supported by the correlation between physiological depression (Figure 5E-F) and symptom reduction (Figure 5H-I). However, the causal relationship is inferred rather than directly demonstrated. The therapeutic effect is modest and from a single session, so claims about optimizing patterns (C178) are somewhat speculative but reasonable as future directions.

results.result: DN neurons in Gnal+/- mice do not show the increased firing irregularity characteristic of other dystonia models. Unlike DYT1, DYT12, DYT6, and dt rat models where cerebellar nuclei show increased discharge irregularity, Gnal+/- mice showed no genotype difference in DN firing regularity under oxotremorine.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C135 are supported by Figure 4 supplement 2B showing no genotype difference in CVisi. The comparison to other models (C133) is appropriately cited. The interpretation (C134-C135) that this reflects a primarily striatal rather than cerebellar origin of dystonia in this model is reasonable speculation supported by the pharmacological induction mechanism.

results.result: Naive Gnal+/- mice do not show hypermetabolism comparable to DYT1/DYT6 patients, but exhibit anomalously high responsiveness of VAL neurons to cerebellar stimulation, likely resulting from increased synaptic transmission or postsynaptic excitability rather than increased DN output.
results.evaluation: Claims C128-C129 are supported by the baseline firing rate data (Figure 2 supplement 2A) showing no difference, combined with enhanced evoked responses (Figure 2 supplement 2C). The inference about synaptic/postsynaptic mechanisms (C129) is reasonable given that DN responsiveness was similar between genotypes, though direct evidence for the mechanism is lacking.

results.result: θ-burst stimulation effects occur downstream of DN. In WT mice, θ-burst stimulations induce lasting potentiation in downstream structures without affecting DN responses, indicating effects occur either as increased thalamic excitability or potentiation of cerebello-thalamic synapses. In Gnal+/- mice, failure to potentiate in saline could result from saturation.
results.evaluation: Claims C146-C148 are supported by data showing no change in DN responses but potentiation downstream (Figures 3-4). However, C147 about the specific mechanism (thalamic excitability vs. synaptic potentiation) cannot be distinguished with the current data. C149 about saturation is speculation, albeit reasonable given the elevated baseline in Post-Oxo mice.

results.result: θ-burst stimulation in oxotremorine induces depression only in Gnal+/- mice, consistent with an abnormal cerebello-thalamic state or sensitivity to cholinergic excitation. This genotype-specific depression contrasts with the lack of effect in WT mice under the same conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C150-C151 are supported by Figure 5E-F showing clear genotype differences. The interpretation of 'abnormal state or sensitivity' (C151) is appropriately cautious, acknowledging that the mechanism could involve either altered baseline state or differential response to cholinergic modulation. The finding is robust and statistically significant.

results.result: Short-latency responses in DLS following DN-CL stimulation are consistent with disynaptic cerebello-striatal connections. θ-burst DN stimulation induces potentiation of fast-spiking striatal neurons in WT mice, potentially through CL potentiation or striatal-level plasticity, though CL-striatal afferents are reportedly less prone to plasticity.
results.evaluation: Claims C161-C163 are supported by Figure 4F-J showing short-latency responses and potentiation in WT mice. The anatomical interpretation (C161-C162) is well-supported by citations. However, the mechanistic speculation (C164-C165) about whether potentiation occurs at CL or striatal level cannot be resolved with the current data and appropriately remains speculative.

results.result: The Gnal+/- mouse model recapitulates key features of DYT25 dystonia. These mice carry a heterozygous Gnal knockout causing reduced striatal cAMP production and disrupted striatal function. Young mice are asymptomatic but develop dystonic symptoms upon oxotremorine administration (systemically or striatally but not cerebellally), which are prevented by muscarinic antagonists.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C3, C26-C34 accurately describe the established model characteristics from Pelosi et al., 2017. These are appropriately cited background claims that establish the validity of the model. The current study replicates the key inducibility features (C3, C32, C83-C84), confirming the model's reliability.

results.result: The study demonstrates that young Gnal+/- mice provide a model of presymptomatic dystonia with pharmacological control over disease states. This allows investigation of network alterations across presymptomatic, symptomatic, and asymptomatic states, revealing early cerebello-thalamic abnormalities and supporting the circuit disorder hypothesis.
results.evaluation: Claims C119, C173-C175, and C177 represent valid conclusions about the model's utility and the study's contribution. The ability to pharmacologically switch between states is a genuine advantage demonstrated by the experimental design. The finding of early cerebello-thalamic abnormalities (C176) in a model with primary striatal dysfunction (C175) does support the circuit disorder view (C177).

results.result: Background on dystonia pathophysiology and prior work. Dystonia is characterized by involuntary movements from muscle co-contraction. The field has evolved from focusing on basal ganglia to recognizing multi-regional dysfunction. Genetic models show endophenotypes, cerebellar dysfunction, and cerebello-thalamic disruptions, with evidence for circuit-level pathophysiology.
results.evaluation: Claims C11-C25, C35-C38 are appropriately cited background claims establishing the scientific context. These are well-supported by the cited literature and accurately represent the current understanding of dystonia as a circuit disorder. They provide essential justification for investigating cerebello-thalamic pathways in the DYT25 model.

results.result: Background on DYT25 genetics, Gα(olf) expression, and developmental considerations. DYT25 is adult-onset with variable penetrance, caused by Gnal mutations affecting the cAMP pathway. Gα(olf) expression changes developmentally, suggesting roles in circuit maturation. Related genes (Gγ7, ADCY5) also cause movement disorders.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C118 are well-cited background information establishing the genetic and molecular basis of DYT25. The developmental expression patterns (C109-C112) and the inference about circuit development (C113) are appropriately cited. C114 is labeled as speculation, which is appropriate. The genotype-phenotype correlations (C115-C117) support the model's relevance.

results.result: Background on dystonia endophenotypes in humans. Various physiological markers (TDT, cortical organization, inter-hemispheric inhibition, hypermetabolism, tract integrity) have been identified in dystonia patients and non-manifesting carriers, though specificity is sometimes limited. Tract integrity patterns may relate to symptom manifestation.
results.evaluation: Claims C120-C127 are appropriately cited background on human endophenotypes. The discussion of specificity issues (C123-C124) is important context. C127 about protective effects of reduced thalamo-cortical connectivity is appropriately labeled as speculation from the cited study and provides important context for interpreting the current findings.

results.result: Discussion of cerebello-thalamic connectivity in dystonia patients and models. Studies show variable findings, with some suggesting reduced cerebellar entrainment of downstream regions. The functional state may depend on dystonia type, with hyperexcitability potentially indicating susceptibility in striatal-origin dystonia, while decreased connectivity might be protective or adaptive.
results.evaluation: Claims C130-C145 appropriately discuss the complexity and variability in the literature on cerebello-thalamic function in dystonia. The citations are appropriate and the interpretations (C143-C145) are cautious, acknowledging uncertainty and alternative explanations. C140 and C145 are appropriately labeled as speculation, and C144 represents a reasonable interpretation of the current findings in context.

results.result: Background on plasticity deficits and therapeutic approaches in dystonia. Impaired plasticity is a hallmark of dystonia at multiple levels. Cerebellar stimulation approaches show variable efficacy in patients, with transcranial θ-burst generally failing to restore cerebellar influence but showing mild improvements with repeated sessions, while deep brain stimulation shows promise.
results.evaluation: Claims C152-C159 provide well-cited background on plasticity and therapeutic approaches. The citations are appropriate and the summary accurately reflects the mixed results in the literature. C159 about repeated sessions is appropriately cautious. This background effectively motivates the therapeutic experiments in the current study.

results.result: Background on striatal plasticity defects in dystonia models. DYT1 and DYT25 models show impaired cortico-striatal LTD, which can be rescued pharmacologically. CL inputs shift plasticity toward LTP, suggesting that increased DN-CL excitability after dystonia onset could help maintain potentiated cortico-striatal synapses.
results.evaluation: Claims C166-C171 are well-cited background on striatal plasticity in dystonia models. C172 represents reasonable speculation linking the cerebello-thalamic findings to known striatal plasticity deficits, though it's appropriately labeled as speculation. This provides important context for understanding how cerebello-thalamic and striatal dysfunctions might interact.

results.result: Anatomical background on cerebello-thalamic and cerebello-striatal pathways. The DN is the main cerebellar output to thalamus, projecting to both VAL and CL. The cerebello-CL-striatal pathway plays a central role in certain forms of dystonia.
results.evaluation: Claims C59, C60, and C70 are well-established anatomical facts appropriately cited from the literature. These provide essential background for interpreting the functional connectivity experiments and justify the choice of recording sites.
